description: We’re ARTICXCODERS, building EarthEcho for NASA’s Earth Information Jukebox challenge. We turn Earth visuals and data into sound to make science engaging and accessible. We’re looking for teammates interested in web development, UI/UX, data visualization, Earth science, or audio programming. Join us to experiment, learn, and build an interactive demo together. Beginners are welcome!
summary:
EarthEcho is an interactive Earth Jukebox that pairs NASA Earth Information Center visualizations with sound generated during playback. Built by ARTICXCODERS, it lets users explore GEDI forest-height visualizations from California, Florida, and Senegal and compare two selected image areas through stereo or alternating audio.

The application estimates canopy height from each visualization’s color scale and maps those estimates to pitch. Soft ticks indicate increasing matched-pixel coverage. A sound legend, narrated explanations, numeric readouts, and listening challenges help users interpret the experience.

EarthEcho explores how sound can provide another way to engage with Earth science. It includes keyboard controls, audio-only viewing, adjustable sound layers, and downloadable sound postcards. The interface explains that rendered-image estimates are approximate and affected by lighting, perspective, and camera movement.
details:
What we built

EarthEcho is a browser-based application that combines NASA Earth Information Center imagery with interactive sonification. Users select a GEDI close-up visualization from California, Florida, or Senegal and compare two image areas.

How it works

The application samples the currently displayed video frame using Canvas. It compares selected pixels with a palette sampled from the corresponding NASA colorbar, rejects background and ambiguous colors, and calculates an approximate median color-derived height.

Each visualization has its own source scale. EarthEcho converts the resulting estimates into a shared audio range, mapping 0–50 meters to 180–720 hertz at the default sensitivity. Higher estimates produce higher tones, with values above 50 meters capped. Pitch smoothing reduces abrupt changes.

Area A and Area B can play through separate stereo channels, alternate, or play individually. Soft ticks indicate an increase in matched-pixel coverage. Areas with insufficient matching pixels become silent.

Interaction and learning

Users can choose preset areas, draw custom image selections, inspect numeric estimates and charts, and explore an interactive sound legend. Narrated explanations, listening challenges, and science questions explain the relationship between imagery and sound.

The application supports keyboard operation, audio-only viewing, high contrast, frozen visual motion, and adjustable sound layers. Users can save bookmarks and export screenshots, comparison reports, audio snapshots, and video postcards.

Tools and implementation

EarthEcho uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript modules, Canvas, Web Audio, browser speech synthesis, MediaRecorder, and a service worker for optional offline caching. Node.js provides the local demonstration server. NASA media assets are bundled with the project.

Scientific considerations

Rendered colors provide approximate estimates, affected by lighting, compression, perspective, and masking. Matching-pixel coverage represents a visualization proxy rather than counted GEDI observations. Screen selections do not track fixed geographic plots, and the sequence reveals observation coverage rather than forest growth.

Intended impact

EarthEcho aims to make Earth science more engaging through combined visual, auditory, and textual exploration. Testing with intended users remains necessary to evaluate accessibility and learning benefits
